question: What is light?
teaser: Meet light as a wave with a colour, see why hot things and single atoms give it out in different ways, and follow a photon into the eye.

stops.title: Sunlight
text: Sunlight lights the park and warms the grass, and everything you see, you see by light that bounced off it or came from it. This light left the Sun about 8 minutes and 20 seconds ago, which is the 150 million kilometres to Earth divided by the speed of light. In empty space light always moves at 299,792,458 metres per second, whatever its colour. But what is it?
stops.notice: Look at the shadows. In air light travels in straight lines, which is why shadows have sharp edges.

stops.title: A wave
text: Light is a wave of electric and magnetic fields, called an electromagnetic wave. The distance from one crest of the wave to the next is its wavelength. Visible light runs from about 400 nanometres (violet) to about 700 nanometres (red), and your eye sees each wavelength as a colour.
Your phone sends and receives the same kind of wave with much longer wavelengths: Wi-Fi at 2.4 gigahertz has a wavelength of about 12 centimetres, the speed of light divided by the frequency.
stops.notice: In the card, find the visible band. It is a thin slice of one long spectrum of waves, from radio to gamma rays.

stops.title: The glow of hot matter
stops.text: Most light around us, including sunlight, is the glow of hot matter. Anything hot gives out light of many wavelengths at once, and the hotter it is, the bluer the mixture. The Sun's surface is at about 5,772 kelvin, and its glow is strongest near 500 nanometres, but it covers all the visible colours, which together look white.
stops.model: The Sun in this view is a model drawn from real size and temperature; the colours are not what you would see.
stops.notice: Open the card for hot glow. A heated metal goes red, then white, as it gets hotter, for the same reason.

stops.title: An atom gives out one colour
text: A single atom of a gas can give out light in a different way, in sharp lines of one colour. A hydrogen atom's electron can only have certain amounts of energy. When it drops to a lower amount, the atom gives out one packet of light carrying exactly the energy lost, and a bigger drop gives a bluer colour. The drop from the third level to the second gives the red line of hydrogen, at a wavelength of about 656 nanometres in air.
stops.model: Bohr's 1913 picture, with the electron on circles, is a simple model that works for hydrogen but fails for atoms with more electrons. The real atom is the cloud in the quantum view.
stops.notice: Choose two levels, such as 3 and 2, and press "Let it jump and emit light". Watch the packet of light leave and compare its colour with the matching line in the spectrum bar.

stops.title: Light comes in packets
text: Light is given out and taken in as packets of energy called photons. A photon has no mass and no electric charge, and in empty space it always moves at 299,792,458 metres per second. Its energy is greater for a shorter wavelength: a violet photon carries about 1.7 times the energy of a red one. Light spreads and interferes like a wave, yet it is emitted and absorbed one photon at a time, and quantum theory describes both.
stops.model: A map of the particles. Positions are a diagram, and the sizes mean nothing.
stops.notice: Find the photon among the force carriers: it also carries the electric and magnetic forces between charged particles.

stops.title: The eye catches photons
text: The eye focuses light onto the retina at the back, which has about 90 million rods and about 5 million cones, counts that differ from person to person. Cones give colour and fine detail in bright light, and there are three kinds. A light-sensing cell responds when a pigment molecule in it absorbs a photon.
stops.notice: Look at the layers at the back of the eye cut open.

stops.title: A molecule that changes shape
text: This is retinal, the light-sensitive part of the visual pigment in your eye. When it absorbs a photon, the molecule flips from a bent shape to a straighter one in about a trillionth of a second. That change starts a chain of signals that ends in a nerve impulse to your brain, and you see.
stops.model: A ball-and-stick picture of one molecule. Bond lengths are true, but the atoms are drawn smaller than their real size so that the bonds show, and the colours are a convention, not real colours.
stops.notice: Look at the long chain of alternating bonds. That chain is what lets the molecule take in visible light.

answer: Light is a wave of electric and magnetic fields whose wavelength sets its colour, moving at 299,792,458 metres per second in empty space and given out and taken in as packets called photons. Hot matter glows with a mixture of wavelengths, while single atoms give out single colours.
unknown: Light behaves as a wave in some experiments and as particles in others. The theory that unites the two, quantum electrodynamics, is one of the best tested in science, but what a photon is beyond what the equations say is still argued about.
